body:
The South Korean government is considering creating a support fund that would entrust public pension money to activist private equity funds (PEFs) to promote "bear hug" M&A targeting undervalued companies, according to sources familiar with the matter. While a direct fund using policy capital was also discussed, an indirect investment structure is now seen as the most viable option to avoid legal challenges.

According to reporting by ChosunBiz on the 8th, the government recently discussed the creation of a "bear hug M&A support fund" at a closed-door Cabinet meeting as part of measures to enhance corporate and shareholder value through M&A market revitalization. A bear hug is a strategy in which an acquirer publicly presents a target company with a price above the current stock price and exceptionally favorable terms, pressuring management to enter negotiations. The term draws an analogy to a bear immobilizing its opponent in a tight embrace.

Under current South Korean law, domestic companies have no obligation to disclose acquisition offers or express an opinion even when they receive one. The structure allows majority shareholders to reject proposals favorable to shareholders on grounds such as defending management control and conceal the fact entirely. Without mandatory disclosure requirements, such offers have difficulty positively impacting stock prices, and some companies deliberately keep their stock prices low to reduce inheritance and gift tax burdens.

The government and the ruling party are simultaneously reviewing legislative amendments and PEF outsourced management to block this structurally. The logic is that if the law is changed to require companies to publicly disclose acquisition offers they receive and the reasons for rejection, the true value of companies would be revealed, preventing "deliberate stock price suppression."

Initially, a proposal was floated at the closed-door meeting for the Korea Development Bank to lead the creation of a fund to support M&A financing. However, the Financial Services Commission, its supervisory agency, reportedly expressed reluctance. The reason cited was the uncertain legal basis for a state-run bank to establish a fund for the purpose of stock market revitalization.

Accordingly, the following alternatives have been raised: ▲creating PEFs in the private sector to acquire undervalued companies, and ▲having the National Pension Service entrust investment and management to activist PEFs. This structure would allow public pension funds to indirectly participate in bear hug M&A by allocating capital to PEFs.

In the United States, under SEC regulations (Schedule 14D-9), when an external tender offer is made, the board of directors must express its opinion to shareholders and disclose it within 10 business days. In the United Kingdom, under the UK Takeover Code, a company board that receives an M&A proposal must immediately disclose it and leave the final decision to shareholders.

A representative example occurred in December last year when Warner Bros.' board posted a shareholder letter on its website stating that "fulfilling the merger agreement signed with Netflix is more advantageous than accepting Paramount's tender offer."

The ruling party is pushing for bear hug M&A support legislation, including codifying the tender offer system. It recently recruited former KakaoBank CEO and former lawmaker Lee Yong-woo as head of the "Financial and Capital Market System Improvement Task Force" to overhaul the disclosure system for enhancing corporate value.

A key ruling party official said, "Looking at foreign cases, there are studies showing that the more aggressive M&A is activated, the more stock price suppression decreases, so we are referencing various examples." The official added, "The government is not directly creating a fund with policy capital," and noted, "The party and government discussed bear hugs as part of improving the capital market's constitution, so we are considering various options including the fund."

Note: Companies with PBR below 0.5 are cited as primary candidates, and analysts note that even if actual acquisitions do not materialize, legislation and fund creation alone could pressure companies to change their attitudes.

The presidential office is reportedly placing weight on "enhancing shareholder value" and plans to hold additional policy discussions following the Cabinet meeting. If bear hug institutionalization becomes a reality, expectations are emerging that governance improvement pressure on undervalued companies will intensify and M&A market transaction volume could increase.
